name: Leo Gerald Heffernan

events.title: Led air search for Lt. Alexander Pearson
events.description: As commander of aviation at Fort Bliss he flew to Sanderson, Texas, to direct flying expeditions into the Big Bend and Chihuahua searching for the lost flier Lt. Alexander Pearson

events.title: Led search for Col. Francis Marshall
events.description: Five airplanes under Maj. Heffernan, commanding the 12th Observation Squadron, left Fort Bliss to join the search for Col. Marshall and Lt. Charles L. Webber

events.title: Unofficial world speed record
events.description: 75 miles in 18 minutes (250 mph) with a gale behind him in a sandstorm; flight began at Nogales; record forwarded to the Chief of Air Service but not official

events.title: Transferred from Rantoul (Chanute Field) to the Panama Canal Zone

bioAdditions: Library of Congress Bain News Service glass negative LC-B2-4268-9 shows "Capt. L. G. Heffernan" with three other officers at Wilbur Wright Field, Ohio, in 1917, when he commanded the field (S7); it carries no known restrictions and was downloaded. Contemporary newspapers on Chronicling America add two rescue missions: in Feb 1921, as commander of aviation at Fort Bliss, he directed the air search for Lt. Alexander Pearson, lost over the Big Bend (S1), and in Dec 1922 he led five planes of the 12th Observation Squadron from Fort Bliss to join the search for Col. Francis Marshall (S2). The San Antonio Light of 24 Mar 1923 gives detail of his record flight: 75 miles from Columbus, N.M., to El Paso in 18 minutes in a sandstorm, with a 100-mph upper wind behind him, on a trip that began at Nogales; the record was "not official" (S3). The Evening Star noted his transfer from Rantoul to the Canal Zone in Sept 1930 (S4), and the Washington Times listed him as retired in Sept 1933 (S5). FamilySearch adds that he married Mathilde Payne in Chicago on 24 Dec 1915, and that his second wife Jane Hamilton Davis (1902-1975) was born at Pleasant Hill, Louisiana, and is buried at Arlington; his death (9 Feb 1956, Los Angeles) is backed by a California county death record (S8).

funFacts: Before his 1923 record he twice led air searches for lost army fliers over the Texas-Mexico border (1921, 1922).
researchLogEntry: Round 4: LOC 1917 photo found and downloaded; newspaper accounts of 1921/1922 searches, 1923 flight, 1930 transfer, 1933 retirement.
